explain.say: Your electricity meter counts the energy your home uses in kilowatt-hours, often called units. To find how much you used, the supplier takes the last reading away from the new one.

explain.say: Each unit costs a set price, called the unit rate. If you used 200 units and the rate is 25 pence, that part of the bill is 200 times 25 pence, which is 50 pounds.

faq.q: How does an electricity meter measure use?
faq.a: It measures the current and voltage coming into your home and adds up the energy over time, counting kilowatt-hours. Smart meters send the reading to the supplier automatically.
asks: How do I read my electricity meter?

faq.a: It is the price you pay for each kilowatt-hour of electricity. Some tariffs have one rate all day; others are cheaper at night or at quiet times.
asks: How much does a unit of electricity cost?

faq.a: It is a fixed amount charged for every day you are connected, even if you use no electricity. It covers the cost of the network of wires, meters and keeping the supply running.
asks: Why do I pay even if I use no electricity?

faq.q: How can I lower my electricity bill?
faq.a: Use fewer units: switch off things you are not using, choose efficient LED bulbs and appliances, and wash clothes at lower temperatures. On a time-of-use tariff, run big appliances at cheaper times.
asks: How do I save electricity at home?

faq.q: Which appliances use the most electricity?
faq.a: Anything that heats or cools uses the most: electric heaters, showers, ovens, kettles, tumble dryers and fridge-freezers, which run all day. Lights and phone chargers use far less.
asks: What uses the most electricity in a house?

facts: In Britain, VAT on household energy is charged at a reduced rate of 5 percent.
Electricity bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours, often called units.

quiz.say: You use 100 units of electricity at 30 pence each, with no other charges. What does it cost?
quiz.why: 100 times 30 pence is 3,000 pence, which is 30 pounds.

wrong.1: 3 pounds would be only 10 units at 30 pence.
wrong.2: 130 comes from adding 100 and 30; you multiply units by the price.
